name: message-sequence
intent: Carry a batch of related messages as one ordered group by marking every message with a sequence identifier, a position number and a size or end marker, so the receiver can reorder the parts, detect gaps and act only when the whole group has arrived.
problem: A batch of messages must be handled as one ordered group, but the channel promises neither order nor completeness: a payload may exceed the maximum message size, competing consumers may interleave a group's parts, and a receiver that processes a truncated batch produces wrong results without any error being raised.
context: Message-oriented integration where the unit of work spans several messages: channels with a message-size limit, asynchronous channels that may reorder or duplicate, parallel consumers or partitions on either side, and receivers that must know a group is complete before invoking domain logic. Applies whether the group exists because the data was too large for one message or because a business transaction was deliberately split into parts.
benefits: Arbitrarily large data crosses a channel with a fixed message-size limit, and every part fits the sender's, broker's and receiver's memory budget.
Ordering and completeness become explicit fields of the message contract instead of an assumption about the transport that fails silently under parallelism or retries.
A missing or duplicated part is detectable, so a truncated batch becomes an explicit error (retry, dead letter, fail fast) instead of wrong results.
Groups can be processed in parallel while each group keeps its order - one session, message group or partition per batch.
The three fields are the standard input of existing flow components: a Resequencer reorders by position, an Aggregator joins on a release condition, and Message Expiration bounds incomplete groups.
A sequence identifier doubles as the correlation key for request-reply, so a reply too large for one message can be streamed as a numbered sequence.
tradeoffs: The receiver must keep per-group state (buffer, seen positions, timer) and release it on completion or expiry; without the expiry an abandoned group leaks memory and state forever.
Partial groups are a new failure mode: a missing part stalls the group until a timeout fires, and the record then has to decide between discarding, dead-lettering or re-requesting the batch.
Group size is bounded by the size marker and the receiver's buffer, so the sender must choose a part size that the slowest receiver can hold.
Numbering is application state: a producer restart that resets positions, a duplicate delivery or a resend that reuses a position corrupts reassembly in ways the transport cannot detect.
Fragmentation adds an assembly seam and latency: the group is usable only at the speed of its slowest part, and the parts cross the wire as more, smaller messages with more per-message overhead.

The pattern gives neither exactly-once nor global order: ordering holds inside one channel, partition or session, and duplicates still need an idempotent receiver, so it composes with other patterns rather than replacing them.

participants.responsibility: Splits the data or the business batch into parts, assigns the sequence identifier, the 1-based position numbers and the size or end marker, and sends the parts over the channel.
The three identification fields carried as message metadata - sequence identifier, position identifier, size or end indicator - never as part of the business payload.

Keeps one buffer per sequence identifier, stores parts by position, tolerates duplicates and out-of-order arrival, detects gaps, and releases the group when the size or end marker says it is complete.
Flow component that reorders parts by position (Resequencer) or joins them once a release condition is met (Aggregator); it may be the receiver itself or a downstream processor.
Bounds the lifetime of an incomplete group - timeout, maximum group size, invalid-message or dead-letter route - so abandoned sequences release their state instead of waiting forever.

use_cases: Sending a document or dataset larger than the channel's maximum message size (Kafka max.message.bytes, the 256 KB SQS limit, MQ segment limits) as numbered chunks the receiver concatenates.
A business batch for one aggregate - all lines of an order, all events of one transaction - applied in order and only once the batch is complete.
A reply too large for one message: the result of a request is streamed as a numbered reply sequence correlated back to the request.

Ordered processing with competing consumers: each group is pinned to one consumer (JMS message grouping, Azure Service Bus session, Kafka partition key) so different groups run in parallel while a group stays ordered.
Reassembly across a file transfer or legacy MQ hop where the receiving system must reconstruct the original document before domain logic sees it.
Distributed batch computation whose partial results are collected per sequence identifier and released only when the last part announces itself.
ActiveMQ Classic JMS message groups: assign the same JMSXGroupID to all parts of a business batch so one consumer owns that group while other groups run in parallel.
Azure Service Bus sessions: send related fragments with one SessionId when a receiver needs FIFO processing and per-session ownership for each sequence.
Kafka keyed partitioning: route each sequence with one key to preserve its order within a partition, then reassemble by position when the logical payload spans records.
avoid_when: The payload fits one message and the channel preserves order: a single Document Message or Command Message is simpler - do not number what needs no numbering.
Size is the only problem: pass a Claim Check (store the payload, send a reference) instead of fragmenting and reassembling.
Order does not matter, only completeness: use Splitter plus Aggregator with a correlation identifier and a count, and drop the position numbers.
Both ends share a process with a FIFO queue (asyncio.Queue, System.Threading.Channels, kotlinx Channel): the queue's ordering suffices and sequence fields add nothing.
A framework already implements the group (Spring Integration aggregator/resequencer, Akka grouped, Service Bus sessions, JMS message groups): configure it instead of hand-rolling headers.
The batch is one logical message that only the transport had to split (ZeroMQ multipart frames): the transport already guarantees ordered, atomic reassembly.
anti_patterns: Putting the sequence fields inside the business payload, where translators, routers and filters cannot see them and the domain schema gets polluted.
Assuming the channel preserves order across partitions, sessions or competing consumers and skipping position numbers; the mistake fails silently as soon as consumer or partition counts change.
An unbounded reassembly buffer with no size cap, no group limit and no expiry: one lost part holds memory and state forever, which is both a leak and a denial-of-service surface.
Numbering messages without a sequence identifier, so two batches produced by the same sender interleave into one corrupt group.
Inconsistent position conventions (0-based in one component, 1-based in another, a size that counts from zero) producing phantom gaps or silently dropped parts.
Rebuilding grouping on top of a broker that already provides it (IBM MQ message groups, JMSXGroupID, Service Bus sessions), ending up with two competing ordering mechanisms.
design_principles: Make ordering and completeness explicit in the contract instead of relying on undocumented transport behaviour.
Separate concerns: fragmentation and reassembly are infrastructure; the domain logic receives a complete batch and never sees the parts.
Bound every resource: a group buffer needs a maximum part size, a maximum number of parts and an expiry.
Design for failure: a gap or a timeout is an explicit result (error, retry, dead letter), not an indefinite wait.
Reuse the standard three fields so generic Resequencer, Aggregator and Message Expiration components apply unchanged.
Assume at-least-once delivery: tolerate duplicates and make the release step idempotent.
best_practices: Carry the sequence identifier, the 1-based position and a size or end marker as headers with documented names, types and semantics, and state the convention in the published message contract.
Always include a size or last-message marker; never make the receiver infer the end of a group from a pause in traffic.
Set a group timeout and a maximum group size, and route expired or oversized groups to the invalid message channel or dead-letter queue with the parts received so far.
Pin a group to a single consumer when order matters (message groups, sessions, partition keys) and process different groups concurrently.
Persist or checkpoint reassembly state when receivers can restart, or accept that in-flight groups are lost and keep the producer able to resend.
Make release idempotent and tolerate duplicates and out-of-order arrival, because retries and re-deliveries are normal on messaging channels.
Prefer the platform's grouping feature (broker groups, sessions, framework aggregator) before writing a custom header protocol; hand-roll only where the transport offers nothing.
sources: Hohpe, G. & Woolf, B., Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Message Sequence (Message Construction chapter).
